card.hook: Picture a car gliding past low, earth-coloured shopfronts while a spiral tower rises behind them. That's the Souq Waqif frame everyone wants, and you can get it from the pavement.
card.stand_here: Stand on Jassim Bin Mohammed Street, across the road from the souq, and face east toward the Fanar. Once you're in the Al Souq district, the middle of the souq is about 340 m, roughly a 4-5 minute walk east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the street view. Try 2x if your phone has it, to bring the tower closer to the souq frontage. Inside the alleys, drop to zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the lanterns.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and put the tower on the middle vertical line, so the souq frontage sits evenly on both sides.
card.best_time: Morning, midday and late afternoon give similar light on the street view. For the alleys, come in the evening, when the lanterns light up and the lights glow blue and yellow. Early morning is quieter inside the souq.
card.selfie_here: Try the old well by the Fanar Islamic Cultural Center, tucked among the souq's winding alleys. Use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone offers it) and hold it a little low, so the lanes fill the space over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Always ask before photographing people or shop interiors, including vendors. Leave out government buildings, security staff and anyone praying. Shops and venues inside may have their own rules. One photo-walk guide says the camels at the camel pen bite, so keep your distance.
card.challenge: Wait for a car to drive through your street shot with the tower dead centre, then take a second picture straight down a lantern-lit alley with the walls running to the middle.
card.good_to_know: Souq Waqif means 'the standing market', because traders once set up at the gates to show off their wares. The original buildings date from the late 19th or early 20th century. After a fire in 2003 the souq was rebuilt, finishing in 2008, with the aim of keeping its old look.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Jassim Bin Mohammed Street, across the road from the souq, and face east toward the Fanar. Once you're in the Al Souq district, the middle of the souq is about 340 m, roughly a 4-5 minute walk east.

selfie_spots.why: A guide says the plaza sits in a square surrounded by cafés and restaurants, and the souq's warm, earthy tones form the backdrop there, though that backdrop is described for the sculpture rather than for a selfie.

card.hook: Picture a giant desert rose made of sand-coloured discs, sitting right at the water's edge at the end of Doha's Corniche. From up high you get the whole thing, with the stadium and a park thrown in.
card.stand_here: Go up to the upper floors of Box Park and head for the side of the floor that faces south. The museum lies to the south, so face that way and keep clear of anything in your path.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole panorama, with Ras Abu Aboud Stadium and MIA Park. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the discs closer. Skip 0.5x, because it makes the museum tiny.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the museum on your screen, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sand-coloured discs keep their detail and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go in late afternoon towards sunset, when the discs can pick up a warm glow. Avoid harsh midday light, which flattens the shapes.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie, walk over to the museum itself and stand outside, in front of the building, with the disc-shaped facade filling the frame behind you. Use the front camera, and switch to the wider setting if your phone has one, so the museum fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to take your photo at the roadside pond beside the museum, with you at the water's edge so the building and its reflection sit behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Phones are fine for photos of yourself, friends and family, but inside the museum flash and selfie sticks aren't allowed. Check the museum's opening days and photo rules, and check that Box Park is open. The sun is strong in Doha during the day, so bring sun protection.
card.challenge: Put the museum on one third of your screen, let the stadium or park balance the other, and keep the horizon dead straight. Bonus points if nobody's thumb sneaks into the corner.
card.good_to_know: Architect Jean Nouvel took the desert rose crystal as his inspiration, and the building is made of 539 interlocking discs. At its heart sits the restored early-20th-century palace of Sheikh Abdullah bin Jassim Al Thani. The current museum opened on 28 March 2019, on the site of the earlier museum from 1975.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go up to the upper floors of Box Park and head for the side of the floor that faces south. The museum lies to the south, so face that way and keep clear of anything in your path.

card.hook: Picture a creamy limestone museum sitting all by itself on its own island, with Doha's water laid out in front of it like a welcome mat. That's the view you're here for, and it's a good one.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Corniche at the Dhow Harbour end, east of the Dhow Harbour skyline viewpoint at the northern tip of the harbour. Face the Museum of Islamic Art across the water; it's about 2.5 km to the east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the water, the shoreline and the museum all fit. Then zoom in a little (2x is plenty) to make the museum bigger in the frame. Save 0.5x for when you walk closer to shoot the facade and fountain.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the museum on one of the vertical lines and let the water fill the bottom third; then tap the museum and slide it a little darker so the pale limestone doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Blue hour into the night, or sunset. Whether sunrise or sunset gives the better light is best checked on the day. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your phone against a railing or hold it close to your body to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the outdoor archway of the museum's West Courtyard: use the front camera, and the archway frames the West Bay skyline across the water. Or head to the Dhow Harbour quay edge on the Corniche, face the water and try the front camera at 0.5x so the museum and skyline fit over your shoulder (check the framing on the spot).
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on the quay at the Dhow Harbour edge, and stand in front of them with the water behind you so the museum and skyline fit in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed in the museum's public areas, but flash is typically restricted inside the galleries, so check the signs on site for the current rules.
card.challenge: Take one shot of the museum with a few palm fronds framing the edge, then one with nothing but water in front of it. Which one is your favourite?
card.good_to_know: The museum sits on its own artificial peninsula, about 60 metres off the Corniche, because architect I. M. Pei asked for a stand-alone island so nothing could be built right up against it. He chose creamy limestone for the walls so the stone shows different shades through the day. It opened on 8 December 2008 and reopened after a major renovation in October 2022.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Corniche at the Dhow Harbour end, east of the Dhow Harbour skyline viewpoint at the northern tip of the harbour. Face the Museum of Islamic Art across the water; it's about 2.5 km to the east.

card.hook: Here's a fun one: the ground under your feet wasn't there before somebody built it. The Pearl-Qatar is a man-made island, and the yacht-packed marina at Porto Arabia is its postcard shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in Porto Arabia, on the inner arc of the promenade, and face the marina mouth. The Pearl-Qatar itself lies about 734 m to the south-east, and from your spot the boats and towers all sit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the marina, boats and towers together. Go to 0.5x for more of the curving promenade and sky. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out one yacht or a cluster of tower lights.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the waterline on the lower third, then tap the brightest part of the water or sky and drag the slider down a touch to make it darker so the tower lights don't blow out.
card.best_time: Aim for blue hour, roughly 30 to 45 minutes after sunset. The water goes glassy and the tower lights reflect in it. As it gets dark, switch on night mode, rest your elbows on the railing and hold still until the shot finishes.
card.selfie_here: On the inner arc of the Porto Arabia promenade, face the yachts and towers so they fill the background behind you. For a different look, try a pedestrian bridge over the Qanat Quartier canal with the pastel buildings behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x and keep the landmark over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: At Qanat Quartier, stand beside the canal near the replica Rialto Bridge and ask a passer-by to stand across the water, so the bridge, canal and pastel buildings all fit in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Avoid photographing security or government facilities. There's no charge for the viewpoint, but check the official site before you go in case of any restrictions or events.
card.challenge: Get a boat in the foreground and a tower light reflected in the water, all in one shot. Bonus points if you're in it too.
card.good_to_know: The Pearl-Qatar is an artificial island of nearly 4 square kilometres, with about 32 kilometres of coastline that didn't exist before. It's split into 12 districts, each with its own architectural style. Porto Arabia alone has 31 towers.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Porto Arabia, on the inner arc of the promenade, and face the marina mouth. The Pearl-Qatar itself lies about 734 m to the south-east, and from your spot the boats and towers all sit in one frame.

card.hook: Everything in Katara is sandy and low and calm, and then you turn a corner and there's a turquoise-tiled dome that looks like someone turned the colour up. Guides call it one of the most photographed spots in the village, and it's easy to see why.
card.stand_here: Stand on the main plaza side of Katara Mosque, outside the building, and face the tiled dome and minaret. From the plaza you can fit both into one upright frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the dome and minaret together. If you're close and the minaret won't fit, tap 0.5x. Then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for a frame filled with tilework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the minaret up with a vertical line so it doesn't lean, then leave a little sky above it.
card.best_time: Late afternoon. The sun hits the tiles head-on, so the blues look their richest.
card.selfie_here: Try the upper stone seats of Katara Amphitheatre, with the sea side of the venue behind you. Or stand in front of the mud-brick Pigeon Towers, near the mosque. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x and keep the landmark over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo from a higher point on the Katara Hills walking paths, where the amphitheatre, the mosques and the sea all sit in the view.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are not allowed inside the mosque, and visitors outside prayer times must follow dress rules, so keep your phone for the outside. Personal photos are generally fine, but commercial photography needs approval from management, and event days may limit photography, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one plaza shot with people crossing and one without, then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: Katara opened in 2010 and is built to look like a traditional Qatari village, with shaded alleys and courtyards. The mosque was designed by the Turkish architect Zainab Fadil Oglu. Leave time to wander: there's a 5,000-seat marble amphitheatre and brick-and-clay pigeon towers about 15 metres high.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the main plaza side of Katara Mosque, outside the building, and face the tiled dome and minaret. From the plaza you can fit both into one upright frame.

card.hook: The bay curves away in front of you, the towers sit above the water, and there's a whole seven kilometres of open space to play with. Don't plant your feet in one spot, because the view changes as the curve does.
card.stand_here: Head for Dhow Harbour, 298 m to the east, about 5 minutes on foot, and stand at the northern tip of the harbour. Face east across the water toward the Museum of Islamic Art, with the moored dhows in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the curve of the bay and the skyline together. Try 0.5x to catch the whole length of the promenade, then 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out single towers across the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the upper or lower line, and use the railing or the edge of the path to lead the eye into the picture.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually softer on the light and kinder to your walking legs. Once the city lights come on in the evening, switch to night mode and hold your elbows tight against your body.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie at the Dhow Harbour waterfront, with the boats in front of you and the skyline behind. The Pearl Monument at the harbour entrance is another popular spot to pose. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the skyline fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand at the tip of the crescent in MIA Park next to the Museum of Islamic Art, and ask a passer-by to frame you with the wider promenade and skyline behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Take care with the traffic when you cross the road. Events can close sections of the Corniche, so check the official site if you're visiting on a special occasion.
card.challenge: Find a railing or path edge that leads straight toward the towers, line your horizon up on a gridline, and see if you can keep it perfectly level.
card.good_to_know: The Corniche follows the curve of Doha Bay and is also where Qatar holds big public events, including the National Day Parade. Much of the land here was reclaimed from the sea from the late 1960s onwards. The Sheraton opened in February 1982 on a specially made island, and the brutalist Central Post Office from 1988 is another landmark along the way.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Dhow Harbour, 298 m to the east, about 5 minutes on foot, and stand at the northern tip of the harbour. Face east across the water toward the Museum of Islamic Art, with the moored dhows in front of you.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found describes the Corniche promenade itself as the backdrop for a selfie, so the selfie spots are the nearest named points where the skyline, dhows and promenade show behind the visitor; these are less exact than the brief asks. No page stated rules about selfie sticks or tripods for this area; one photography guide only mentions photographers setting up tripods along the waterfront, which is not a rule. card.hook: The stadium is about 388 metres across, so stand too close and you'll spend ten minutes backing up and still miss half of it. Aspire Park fixes that with a big green lawn and the whole district in one shot.
card.stand_here: Head to the walkway below the Aspire Tower in Aspire Park, in the Aspire Zone, Al Rayyan. From here the stadium lies to the east, so face east with the park's grass in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the lawn, the tower and the stadium in together. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the arches and the roof line.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the tower and arches upright, then put some grass or path in the bottom third and leave a little sky above.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is your friend, with softer light and cooler air for strolling round the park. Midday sun is harsh and can leave the sky looking washed out.
card.selfie_here: Wander the open park grounds around the stadium and turn your back to it. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the stadium fits over your shoulder. The park is big and we don't have one special spot for you, so pick a patch of lawn or a path you like.
card.rules_and_safety: Aspire Park is an open public space, but access to the stadium and to The Torch Doha can vary, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the tower and the arches both stand perfectly straight on the gridlines, with a strip of grass at the bottom. Bonus points if nobody walks through it.
card.good_to_know: Khalifa International Stadium first opened in 1976 and was rebuilt for the 2022 FIFA World Cup, reopening in 2017 with 45,857 seats and a roof over the whole bowl. Its two tall arches, one on the east side and one on the west, are each over 120 metres high, so you can spot the stadium from far away. It hosted eight matches at the 2022 World Cup, including the third-place play-off.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the walkway below the Aspire Tower in Aspire Park, in the Aspire Zone, Al Rayyan. From here the stadium lies to the east, so face east with the park's grass in front of you.

selfie_spots.detail: in the park grounds around the stadium (the sources do not name a specific path or spot inside it)
selfie_spots.why: The stadium is described as surrounded by a large public park with walking trails, which gives open ground for a selfie with the stadium behind you.

selfie_research.notes: Weak evidence overall. None of the pages I found names a specific spot where the stadium is behind a visitor, or a spot where a passer-by should photograph a visitor with the whole stadium in frame, so I did not invent one. Aspire Park is the only named place near the stadium that a page links to walking or park space, and the 'selfie with stadium behind' framing is my inference from that. Other pages name the stadium's dual arches and night lighting as photo subjects (airial.travel, aroundtheworld4u.com) without a location. Villagio Mall is described as across the street from the stadium (sumfinity.com), but no page calls it a photo spot. No page states selfie stick or tripod rules, so the rules list is empty. No safety point was mentioned on the pages I found. The airial.travel page says personal photography is generally allowed inside, but that is not a selfie-stick or tripod rule, so I left it out. Checking a local map or a recent visitor photo guide for a specific stadium-facing spot would be worthwhile.

card.hook: Picture a shaded archway, a spotless modern wall right beside it, and restored courtyard houses just around the corner. That's Msheireb: new and old, side by side, and it looks great on your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand near شارع وادي مشيرب, about 360 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The district opens up in front of you, then you can wander in for closer shots.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in the tall buildings and the full width of the street. Switch to 1x for most shots, then try 2x-5x (depends on your phone) for arches, rooflines and façade details.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on your gridlines and line up the building edges with them so everything stands up straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and cooler walking. After sunset the lit streets look lovely in night mode, so rest your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to Barahat Msheireb square, the open central plaza, and stand with the surrounding buildings and the covered canopy behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x to fit more in) and let the patterned floor and shade do the work. The canopy can be closed or changed on the day, so check when you arrive.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Mosaic terrace at the Mandarin Oriental, looking down over the square, while you stand in the square so the whole space fits in the frame (it's not confirmed that non-guests can go up, so check on arrival).
card.rules_and_safety: Casual personal photography is generally fine, but professional photography or drones may need permits. Museums and individual buildings may have their own rules (flash is reported to be banned at the museums), so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find an archway or shaded passage and get a friend to stroll through it, so the arch becomes your picture frame.
card.good_to_know: Msheireb means 'a place to drink water' in Arabic. The district covers about 31 hectares, and construction began in January 2010. The restored courtyard houses in the Heritage Quarter became the Msheireb Museums, which opened in October 2015.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near شارع وادي مشيرب, about 360 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The district opens up in front of you, then you can wander in for closer shots.

selfie_research.notes: No page found gives a selfie-stick rule. The tripod ban comes from a museum page and may not cover the open square. The Mosaic terrace is described as a viewpoint of the square, but no source confirms that non-guests can access it, so check on arrival. The square spot relies on a 2020 ILoveQatar guide and other sources that are a year or more old; check that the square's current features are still in place. Another source notes the square has a retractable canopy, so it may be closed or changed when you visit. The Airial page lists the Msheireb Tram as a photo spot, but no page gave its location, so I left it out.
